title: Availability, nines, SLI/SLO/error budgets
scopeHtml:
Scope: nines, series and parallel availability, SLI SLO SLA, error budgets and burn rate.

Scope: nines, series and parallel availability, SLI SLO SLA, error budgets and burn rate.

notes.title: What availability means
notes.html:
Availability is the fraction of time (or requests) in which the service works correctly. Availability = uptime / (uptime + downtime). It is usually quoted in "nines".

It is not the same as durability (data is not lost) or reliability in general. S3 is designed for 99.99% availability but 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability: it may be briefly unreachable but should never lose your object.

Worked example. 30-day month = 43,200 minutes. 99.9% availability allows 43.2 minutes of downtime; 99.99% allows 4.3 minutes.

Industry examples. AWS publishes SLAs per service (for example EC2 region-level 99.99%, S3 Standard 99.9%; confirm current SLA pages). Stripe and Google Cloud also publish status and post-mortems.

Everyday analogy. A shop's opening hours: "open 99.9% of the hours it promised".

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing availability with durability.
  • Measuring only server uptime: a server that answers 500s is "up" but not available. Count successful requests.

notes.title: The nines table
notes.html:
Memorise this table.

Availability  Downtime/year   Downtime/month*  Typical meaning
99%           3.65 days       7.2 hours        hobby / batch
99.9%         8.76 hours      43.8 minutes     standard web service
99.95%        4.4 hours       21.9 minutes     managed DB tier
99.99%        52.6 minutes    4.4 minutes      multi-AZ, automated failover
99.999%       5.26 minutes    26 seconds       multi-region, extreme cost
* average month (365 / 12 = 30.4 days). A strict 30-day month gives 43.2 min for 99.9% and 4.3 min for 99.99%.

Decision gravity. The availability target drives architecture: 99.9% can be one region with multi-AZ (reversible, modest cost); 99.99% needs automated failover and careful deploys; 99.999% needs active-active multi-region, which is a one-way door in complexity, data consistency, and cost. Do not promise more than the business pays for. Also your target cannot exceed your dependencies' (next section).

Everyday analogy. Delivery promises: "within a week" is cheap, "within 10 minutes" needs a dark store next door.

Common interview traps.

  • Promising five nines for a normal CRUD app.
  • Forgetting planned maintenance counts unless excluded in the SLA.

notes.title: Availability in series and in parallel
notes.html:
Series (all needed): multiply. Parallel (any one is enough): combine failure probabilities.

Series:   A = A1 x A2 x A3
Parallel: A = 1 - (1 - A1) x (1 - A2)

Worked example (series). LB 99.99%, app 99.95%, DB 99.95%, cache 99.9%: 0.9999 x 0.9995 x 0.9995 x 0.999 = 99.79%, about 18.5 hours of downtime a year, worse than any single part.

Worked example (parallel). Two app instances each 99% available and independent: 1 - 0.01 x 0.01 = 99.99%. Caveat: failures are rarely independent (same deploy, same bug, same AZ), so real gains are lower. Redundancy must be across failure domains (instances, racks, AZs, regions).

Industry examples. AWS places instances across 3 AZs; losing one AZ should keep the service up. Google and Netflix design for region failure for tier-1 services (Netflix regularly evacuates a region).

Everyday analogy. A chain of links is as weak as the weakest; two ropes holding the same weight are safer than one.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing parallel availability as if failures were independent when they share a deploy or a database.
  • Adding a redundant app tier but leaving a single database.

notes.title: SLI, SLO, SLA
notes.html:
SLI is what you measure. SLO is the target you set. SLA is the contract with penalties.

  • SLI (indicator): a ratio, such as good requests / total requests, or fraction of requests under 300 ms.
  • SLO (objective): internal target, such as 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days.
  • SLA (agreement): external promise with refunds, usually looser than the SLO (SLA 99.9%, SLO 99.95%).

Good SLIs: availability (non-5xx / total), latency (requests < 300 ms / total), freshness (data age < 1 min), correctness. Measure at the load balancer or from the client side, not from the server's own health.

Worked example. SLI: sum(rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])). SLO: >= 99.9% over rolling 30 days. If the 30-day ratio is 99.95%, you are within target.

# Illustrative SLO definition (OpenSLO-style, not exact schema)
slo:
  name: checkout-availability
  objective: 99.9
  window: 30d
  sli: good_requests / total_requests

Industry examples. Google's SRE book popularised SLI/SLO/error budget. Cloud SLAs give service credits (for example 10% to 100% of the bill) when the SLA is missed.

Decision gravity. An SLA is a legal one-way door; tightening it later is hard. Set SLOs conservatively first; they are cheap to adjust.

Everyday analogy. SLI is your speedometer, SLO is the speed you aim for, SLA is the fine if you break the limit.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating SLO and SLA as the same.
  • Picking too many SLIs; start with 2 or 3 (availability, latency).
  • Choosing 100% as a target; it is unreachable and blocks all change.

notes.title: Error budgets
notes.html:
Error budget = 1 - SLO. It is the amount of unreliability you are allowed, and you can spend it on releases and experiments.

SLO 99.9% over 30 days  -> budget 0.1% -> 43.2 minutes
Or in requests: 100M requests/month x 0.001 = 100,000 failed requests allowed

Burn rate = how fast the budget is consumed relative to the allowed rate. Burn rate 1 uses the budget exactly at the end of the window; burn rate 14.4 uses a 30-day budget in about 2 days. A common alerting pattern (Google SRE workbook) pages on fast burn over short windows (for example burn 14.4 over 1 h) and tickets on slow burn (burn 1 over 3 days).

Worked example. Budget 43.2 min/month. A bad deploy causes 20 min of errors: 46% of budget gone in one day. Policy: pause risky launches until the budget recovers or a postmortem action is done.

Industry examples. Google SRE teams use budget policies to arbitrate between product velocity and reliability. Many companies track budgets in tools like Prometheus/Grafana, Datadog SLOs or Nobl9.

Decision gravity. A budget policy is an organisational choice and reversible, but it only works if leadership honours the freeze.

Everyday analogy. A monthly allowance: you can spend on risks until it is gone.

Common interview traps.

  • Alerting on raw error spikes instead of burn rate (noisy pages).
  • Having an SLO but no consequence when it is breached.

notes.title: How to reach higher availability
notes.html:
Availability comes from removing single points of failure, shrinking the blast radius of changes, and recovering fast. Two quantities: MTBF (mean time between failures) and MTTR (mean time to repair). Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). Cutting MTTR is usually cheaper than raising MTBF.

Checklist:

  • Redundancy across AZs; stateless tiers behind health-checked LBs.
  • Database replication with automated failover (RPO and RTO stated).
  • Canary and progressive rollouts, feature flags, instant rollback; most outages follow a change.
  • Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, load shedding.
  • Graceful degradation: serve stale cache or a reduced page rather than an error.
  • Runbooks, alerting on SLO burn, regular game days.

Worked example. Failures once a month (MTBF 720 h) with 60 min to repair: A = 720 / 721 = 99.86%. Cutting repair time to 6 min (auto-failover) gives 99.986%, a 10x gain without making the system fail less.

Industry examples. Netflix chaos engineering (Chaos Monkey) validates redundancy; Amazon uses cell-based architectures to limit blast radius.

Everyday analogy. A hospital: spare generators (redundancy), checklists before surgery (safe change), fast ambulance (low MTTR).

Common interview traps.

  • Focusing only on preventing failure; recovery speed often matters more.
  • Forgetting that deployments, not hardware, cause most outages.

notes.title: Counting availability by requests, not minutes
notes.html:
Count what users experience: successful requests divided by valid requests. A time-based number ("up 99.9% of minutes") hides the fact that a 4 am blip costs nothing and the same blip at the Friday dinner rush costs a lot. If 10M orders were attempted in a month and 9.99M succeeded, you are at 99.9%, whichever minutes the failures fell in.

Four rules keep the number honest:

  1. Slow counts as down. Pick a time limit per journey (for example checkout under 2 s) and count anything slower as a failure; users give up long before your server does.
  2. Measure from outside. A dead server cannot report that it is dead, so the dashboard freezes at its last good value. Use load balancer logs or a synthetic probe that places a fake order every minute from another network.
  3. Count only valid requests. A request you correctly reject (bad card number, malformed JSON) is a success, not an error. Server faults (5xx, timeouts) count; client faults (4xx) do not.
  4. Planned maintenance counts as downtime. A single server patched monthly (10 min) and crashing twice a year (60 min each) loses 12 x 10 + 2 x 60 = 240 min of 525,600, so 99.95%, and half of that was chosen by you. The real fix is invisible maintenance, which needs a second copy.

Industry examples. Google's SRE practice defines availability SLIs as good events over valid events; AWS and Stripe publish request-based SLAs. Synthetic probes are what status-page tools run from several regions.

Everyday analogy. A shop is "open" only if you can actually buy something; a door that is unlocked while every till is broken is not open.

Common interview traps.

  • Measuring availability inside the failing server.
  • Counting only 5xx and forgetting timeouts and slow successes.
  • Forgetting that maintenance windows consume the error budget.

notes.title: Static stability: spare capacity that is already running
notes.html:
When a zone dies, the survivors must already be able to carry its traffic, because there is no time to start new servers. Autoscaling takes minutes (boot, warm cache, pass health checks) while the lost traffic arrives in seconds. So you provision the spare room beforehand.

Worked example. Peak load needs 12 servers. With 2 zones, the one survivor must hold all 12, so each zone runs 12 (24 total, 2x). With 3 zones, the two survivors must hold 12 between them, so each zone runs 6 (18 total, 1.5x). Rule of thumb: with N zones you provision N / (N - 1) times peak, so 2 zones cost 2x, 3 zones 1.5x, 4 zones about 1.33x. More zones is cheaper insurance.

Industry examples. AWS's Well-Architected guidance calls this static stability; Netflix runs enough regional headroom to evacuate a failed region.

Common interview traps.

  • Counting on autoscaling to replace a lost zone in time.
  • Sizing for average load rather than peak when a zone is lost.
  • Forgetting that failover traffic also warms cold caches and can overload the database.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Availability = successful requests / total (or uptime fraction); durability is different.
  • Memorise nines: 99.9% = 8.8 h/year; 99.99% = 53 min/year; 99.999% = 5 min/year.
  • Series multiplies (worse); parallel combines (better) if failures are independent.
  • SLI = measure, SLO = internal target, SLA = contract with penalty (looser than SLO).
  • Error budget = 1 - SLO; spend it on change, freeze when gone; alert on burn rate.
  • Raise availability via redundancy, safe deploys and low MTTR; each extra nine costs far more.

questions.promptHtml: What does "availability" mean, and how is it different from durability and from server uptime?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Teams routinely quote server uptime as availability and miss user-visible failure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Availability is the fraction of requests (or time) in which the service gives a correct answer in an acceptable time. Durability is whether stored data survives. Uptime is a weaker measure: a server that is running but returning 500s is "up" and not available. I count successful requests over valid requests, measured from outside.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Availability = uptime / (uptime + downtime)      (time based)
Availability = good requests / valid requests    (request based, preferred)

S3 Standard is designed for 99.99% availability but 11 nines of durability (verify current numbers): it may be unreachable for minutes but should never lose an object. A 30-day month is 43,200 minutes, so 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes down and 99.99% about 4.3 minutes. Request-based counting reflects user pain: a 4 am blip costs little, the same blip at the dinner rush costs a lot, and a time-based number treats them alike.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Confusing availability with durability.
  • Measuring "server is up" rather than successful requests.
  • Counting only 5xx, ignoring timeouts and slow responses.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a slow response count as down? -> Yes if it exceeds the journey's limit (for example checkout 2 s); users leave before your server gives up.
  2. Do 4xx count as failures? -> Correctly rejected client errors do not; server faults do.
  3. Is planned maintenance downtime? -> Yes for the user unless the SLA excludes it; it consumes the error budget.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: uptime percentage. Senior: request-based, outside measurement, slow-counts-as-down and valid-request rules.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Dashboards green from the server's own view while users saw errors at the load balancer.

questions.promptHtml: How much downtime per year do 99.9%, 99.99% and 99.999% allow, and why is each extra nine so expensive?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The table is expected knowledge; the real signal is the cost reasoning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: 99.9% is about 8.8 hours a year, 99.99% about 53 minutes, 99.999% about 5 minutes. Each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime by 10x, which means humans cannot respond in time: you need automated failover, safe deploys, and eventually multi-region active-active, with growing cost and complexity.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
99%      3.65 days/yr   7.2 h/month
99.9%    8.76 h/yr      43.8 min/month
99.95%   4.4 h/yr       21.9 min/month
99.99%   52.6 min/yr    4.4 min/month
99.999%  5.26 min/yr    26 s/month

Rule: your target cannot exceed your dependencies'. 99.9% fits a single region with multi-AZ. 99.99% needs automated failover (a 30 s failover alone spends 12% of a month's 4.4 min budget). 99.999% needs multi-region active-active, which is a one-way door in data consistency and cost.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Promising five nines for a CRUD app.
  • Forgetting maintenance counts.
  • Forgetting that a human paged at 3 am needs minutes just to log in.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 99.95% downtime per month? -> About 21.9 minutes (average month).
  2. Why is MTTR so important at four nines? -> A single 20 minute manual recovery exceeds the monthly budget.
  3. Who pays for the extra nines? -> The business; so you ask what an hour of downtime costs before choosing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: recites the table. Senior: links each nine to an architecture step and to the dependency ceiling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Contracts that promised 99.99% on a system with a single-region database.

questions.promptHtml: Explain SLI, SLO and SLA with an example for a checkout API. Which one should be stricter, and where do you measure the SLI?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Confusing them leads to both unreachable promises and unmeasurable goals.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The SLI is the measured ratio, for example requests that succeed in under 2 s over all valid requests. The SLO is the internal target, say 99.95% over 30 days. The SLA is the external contract with penalties, say 99.9%, deliberately looser than the SLO. I measure at the load balancer or from a synthetic probe outside, never from the server's own health.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SLI: sum(rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
SLO: SLI >= 99.95% over rolling 30 days
SLA: 99.9% or service credits (legal)

Pick 2 to 3 SLIs per journey: availability, latency under threshold, maybe freshness/correctness. An SLO of 100% is unreachable and blocks all change. The gap between SLO and SLA is your safety margin. An SLA is a legal one-way door; SLOs are cheap to tune.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating SLO and SLA as the same number.
  • Dozens of SLIs nobody watches.
  • Measuring from inside the failing process.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you set the first SLO? -> From current performance and user need; start conservative, adjust.
  2. What if the SLO is always met by a wide margin? -> It is probably too loose or you are over-investing; tighten or spend the budget.
  3. How do SLO and error budget relate? -> Budget = 1 - SLO, the allowed unreliability to spend on change.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: three definitions. Senior: gives the query, chooses SLO tighter than SLA, ties it to the budget policy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that signed an SLA equal to their SLO and paid credits after one bad week.

questions.contextHtml: A sales lead wants to promise customers 99.99% for an order API. Architecture: CDN/LB 99.99%, API (3 instances across AZs, each 99.9%), cache 99.9% (needed on every call), single Postgres primary 99.95%, third-party payment provider 99.9% (SLA from them), message queue 99.95% (needed for confirmation).
questions.promptHtml: Can we promise 99.99%? What would you change and what would you tell sales?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Multiplies two numbers, or says "yes, we have three API instances".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is every dependency on the critical path? Can the cache be bypassed? Can payment be asynchronous? Is the 99.99% for all calls or just reads?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; design review.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The serial chain is limited by its weakest and by the product.
  4. How I'd verify (the math): API tier in parallel (assuming independence): 1 - 0.001^3 is about 100%. Series: 0.9999 x 1.0 x 0.999 (cache) x 0.9995 (DB) x 0.999 (payments) x 0.9995 (queue) = about 99.28%, roughly 63 hours a year. So no.
  5. Root cause: Series multiplies; payment at 99.9% alone caps us below 99.99%. Also "independent" is optimistic for instances sharing a deploy.
  6. Fix: Make the cache optional (fallback to DB), accept orders into a durable queue and call the payment provider asynchronously with retries, DB with automatic failover, then recompute. The critical path shrinks to LB, API, DB, queue. Promise 99.9% externally, run 99.95% internally.
  7. Prevention: Keep a dependency table with each SLA and criticality.
  8. Trade-offs: Async payment changes the product (order accepted, payment confirmed later). I would not promise more than the weakest hard dependency.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Payment provider adds a second provider? -> Parallel (needs routing and idempotency), raises ceiling.
  • Failures not independent? -> Real gain is smaller; shared deploy or AZ is a common cause.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promised four nines was found to be bounded by a third-party at three nines; moving it off the critical path fixed the math.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: promises it.
  • Hire: multiplies series and refuses.
  • Strong hire: removes dependencies from the path and sets internal vs external numbers.

questions.subtopic: error budget after a bad deploy
questions.contextHtml: SLO: 99.9% over 30 days, about 100M requests/month. On day 9 a deploy caused 12 minutes of 30% errors at the average rate of 2,300 req/s. Before that day the budget used was 15,000 failed requests. The product manager wants to ship a risky migration on day 12.
questions.promptHtml: How much budget is left and what do you advise?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "We were only down 12 minutes, so we are fine", with no arithmetic or policy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the budget request-based? Is there a written budget policy? Was the cause fixed? Is the migration reversible?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Confirm the rollback worked; stop further risky changes today.
  3. Hypotheses: Not applicable; compute.
  4. How I'd verify: Budget = 100M x 0.001 = 100,000 failed requests. Incident failures: 720 s x 2,300 req/s = 1,656,000 requests, x 0.30 = 496,800 failures. That exceeds the whole budget (100,000) by about 5x, so the SLO is already breached this window.
  5. Root cause (of my advice): Budget is exhausted; the policy says freeze risky launches.
  6. Fix: Freeze non-essential change, fix reliability debt, run the postmortem, add canary and automatic rollback; allow the migration only if it reduces risk or is reversible and gated with a canary after leadership agrees.
  7. Prevention: Burn-rate alerts would have paged within minutes: the incident burned about 5x the monthly budget in 12 minutes (a burn rate in the thousands, far above the 14.4 fast-burn page threshold).
  8. Trade-offs: A freeze costs feature velocity; ignoring it makes the SLO meaningless. I would not hide the number or restate the SLO retroactively.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Traffic was 20% lower so failures differ? -> Recompute; the conclusion barely changes.
  • Error-budget policy does not exist? -> Write one with leadership sign-off.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team that honoured its freeze after one deploy incident shipped a canary system within two weeks and cut deploy incidents by half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no arithmetic.
  • Hire: shows the budget is gone and applies policy.
  • Strong hire: adds burn-rate alerting, canary and a negotiation of the migration.

questions.contextHtml: The team reports 99.99% availability last month. The calculation: each app server exposes /health returning 200 when the process is up, scraped every 30 s; availability = fraction of scrapes returning 200. Customers complained about 20 minutes of failed checkouts on the 14th: the app was up but a bad config made every POST /checkout return 502 from the gateway, and the DB was timing out for 3 minutes on the 21st. Monthly patching of the single instance took 10 min on the 3rd. The status page showed all green.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with the measurement and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more health checks", still measured from inside.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which journeys matter? What is the latency limit per journey? Do we have LB logs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Report the honest number for the postmortem.
  3. Hypotheses (flaws): (a) health endpoint does not test the journey; (b) measured by the failing process; (c) timeouts and slow responses ignored; (d) maintenance excluded without agreement; (e) sampled every 30 s.
  4. How I'd verify: Recompute from LB logs: failed checkouts over valid checkouts. Roughly 20 + 3 + 10 = 33 minutes bad out of 43,200 = 99.92%, not 99.99%.
  5. Root cause: The SLI does not reflect what users do.
  6. Fix: SLI = non-5xx and under-2 s requests over valid requests at the LB; add a synthetic probe placing a test order every minute from outside; count 4xx as success only if correct; maintenance counts.
  7. Prevention: Alerts on the SLI itself and on probe failure.
  8. Trade-offs: Honest numbers look worse; that is the point. I would not keep a vanity metric.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Dead server cannot report itself? -> Right; that is why the probe runs elsewhere.
  • Should synthetic traffic count? -> Report it separately, and do not let it pollute capacity metrics.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "four nines" report was replaced by LB-based numbers and revealed three nines; the investment case that followed was approved.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks health check.
  • Hire: moves to request-based SLI from LB.
  • Strong hire: adds synthetic probe, slow-as-down, maintenance rule.

questions.promptHtml: What is an error budget, what is burn rate, and why alert on burn rate instead of raw error counts?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can turn an SLO into a decision tool and sane paging.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The error budget is 1 minus the SLO: the unreliability I am allowed to spend on releases and experiments. For 99.9% over 30 days that is 43.2 minutes, or 100,000 failed requests out of 100M. Burn rate is how fast I consume it relative to an even spend: rate 1 exhausts it exactly at the window's end, rate 14.4 exhausts it in about 2 days. I page on fast burn over short windows and ticket on slow burn, so alerts track real SLO risk, not noise.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
budget = 1 - SLO                       99.9% -> 0.1%
burn   = observed error rate / budget  error 1.44% / 0.1% = 14.4
30 days / 14.4 = about 2.1 days to exhaustion
Page:   burn >= 14.4 over 1 h (and 5 min to confirm)
Ticket: burn >= 1 over 3 days

This follows the Google SRE workbook pattern (multi-window, multi-burn-rate; verify the exact thresholds for your SLO). The budget policy is the human part: when it is exhausted, freeze risky launches and spend on reliability. Without a consequence the SLO is decoration.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Paging on every error spike; most spikes burn nothing meaningful.
  • An SLO with no policy when it is breached.
  • Using a single long window: slow to detect and slow to reset.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a short confirm window too? -> It stops the alert from staying red after the incident has ended.
  2. What if the budget is never used? -> The SLO may be too loose or the team too cautious; spend it on faster releases.
  3. How does budget interact with an SLA? -> The SLA is looser; hitting SLO miss does not always mean penalties, but you are near them.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "allowed downtime". Senior: burn-rate alert thresholds, windows, and the policy for freezing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams cut pages by about an order of magnitude by moving from threshold alerts to burn alerts.

questions.contextHtml: A service fails about once a month (MTBF 720 h). Each failure takes 60 minutes to repair: page, log in, diagnose, restart or fail over by hand. Availability target is 99.99%. Two proposals, each costing about the same: (A) rewrite risky modules and add tests aiming to double MTBF; (B) automate failover, add a runbook-driven auto-restart and better alerting, aiming at a 6 minute repair.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you choose and why? Show numbers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks A because "preventing failures is better than reacting", with no arithmetic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What causes the failures: code, hardware, deploys? Can they be automatically recovered? Do failures vary in severity?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Start with detection and a runbook; it helps both options.
  3. Hypotheses: Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
  4. How I'd verify (math): Today 720 / 721 = 99.861%. Option A: MTBF 1,440 h gives 1,440 / 1,441 = 99.931%. Option B: MTTR 0.1 h gives 720 / 720.1 = 99.986%. Neither reaches 99.99% alone; B is 10x less downtime than today, A is only 2x.
  5. Root cause of the gap: Repair time is the larger, more controllable term.
  6. Fix: Do B first, then add A where failure causes are known; for 99.99% also reduce failure impact with redundancy so most failures cost seconds, not minutes, and cut deploy-caused failures with canaries.
  7. Prevention: Track MTTR by phase (detect, diagnose, mitigate).
  8. Trade-offs: Automated failover can cause split brain or flapping; test it. I would not claim four nines from MTTR work alone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Failures are rare but catastrophic (data loss)? -> Then prevention and backups dominate.
  • Failures are mostly deploys? -> Canary and instant rollback attack both terms.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team halved its incident minutes by adding auto-rollback; it never touched the bug count.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chooses A on intuition.
  • Hire: computes and picks B.
  • Strong hire: includes detection time, redundancy, and risks of auto-failover.

questions.contextHtml:
Peak load needs 20 servers of capacity. Today the service runs in 2 zones with 14 servers each (28 total, 70% utilisation each at peak) with autoscaling that needs about 5 minutes (boot, warm cache, health check). Zone B loses power. Metrics at +30 s:

zone A: 14 servers, CPU 140% demand -> 100% pegged, queue growing
p99: 120 ms -> 4.5 s ; 5xx 38% ; autoscaler: launching 12 instances (ETA 5 min)

The capacity planner asks how it should have been sized.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what happened and the right sizing for 2 zones vs 3 zones.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Autoscaling will fix it in 5 minutes", ignoring that 5 minutes of 38% errors blows the budget and cold caches then hit the DB.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we shed load or degrade now? Is the DB ready for the shifted traffic and cold caches? Do we have pre-warmed capacity?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed non-critical traffic, enable degraded mode, raise the autoscaler's launch rate, protect the DB with limits.
  3. Hypotheses: Not applicable; the math is the cause. Surviving zone carries 28 x 0.7 = 19.6 servers-worth of work on 14 servers = 140%.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare zone utilisation before the incident; static stability rule N/(N-1) x peak.
  5. Root cause: The spare room was not already running; autoscaling is too slow for a zone loss.
  6. Fix: With 2 zones each must hold the full peak: 2 x 20 = 40 servers (2x). With 3 zones the survivors must hold 20 between two: 10 each plus headroom, so 30 servers (1.5x), and survivors would be at 100% of peak unless I add margin, so I would target about 36 (3 x 12): survivors at 83%. More zones is cheaper insurance (4 zones: 1.33x).
  7. Prevention: Run a zone-evacuation game day; alert on "capacity after losing the biggest zone".
  8. Trade-offs: 1.5x to 2x costs money every day; the alternative is outage minutes. I would not rely on autoscaling for zone loss, but I would still use it for growth.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Three zones but the DB is single-zone? -> The DB is the SPOF; the 3-zone app buys nothing.
  • Cold caches after failover? -> Warm standby caches or rate-limit refill so the DB survives.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A zone loss at 70% per-zone CPU doubled the survivors' load; the team moved to three zones at 55% and zone loss became a non-event.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: relies on autoscaling.
  • Hire: explains the 140% and sizes N/(N-1).
  • Strong hire: includes DB, cold caches, shedding and game day.

questions.contextHtml: An enterprise prospect, worth about 30% of next year's revenue, demands a 99.99% availability SLA with service credits of 100% of monthly fees if breached. Current performance on the platform over 12 months: 99.93% measured at the load balancer. Architecture is a single region with multi-AZ and a Postgres primary with manual promotion. Sales says "just sign it".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Signs, or flatly refuses without options.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How is availability measured and by whom? Which endpoints are in scope? Are maintenance windows excluded? What is the penalty cap and measurement window (monthly)? Is the customer's need really 99.99% or fast recovery?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not sign today.
  3. Hypotheses: Gap: 99.93% is about 30 min/month; 99.99% allows about 4.3 min/month.
  4. How I'd verify: Review last 12 months of incidents: how many would have breached? Count failover time: manual promotion alone costs 10 minutes or more.
  5. Root cause (of the gap): Manual recovery and single-region design cap us near three nines.
  6. Fix (options): (a) Offer 99.9% with credits scaled to impact; (b) offer 99.99% only for a narrowed scope (read API) with defined exclusions and capped credits; (c) fund the work: automated failover, canary deploys, tested restores, possibly multi-region, with a cost and timeline estimate before signing.
  7. Prevention: SLA authored with engineering, measured from the LB, written exclusions.
  8. Trade-offs: An SLA is a legal one-way door; a lost deal is recoverable, uncapped 100% credits might not be. I would not sign a number I cannot measure.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Customer insists? -> Price it: higher tier fee covering the investment, with a ramp-up period.
  • Can we exclude planned maintenance? -> Often negotiable if announced, but verify what the contract defines.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A company signed a four-nine SLA on a three-nine system and paid credits for three quarters while building the failover it should have built first.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sign or refuse.
  • Hire: measures the gap and counter-offers.
  • Strong hire: scopes, caps credits, prices the investment, defines measurement.

questions.contextHtml:
The design doc claimed: two app instances at 99% each in parallel give 99.99%. Last Tuesday both instances went down for 41 minutes after a deploy introduced a null pointer on a rarely used code path, hit by a nightly job. Logs:

14:02:11 deploy v412 rolled to app-1 and app-2 (both, 30 s apart)
14:09:40 NullPointerException OrderMapper.map(OrderMapper.java:88)  app-1
14:09:52 NullPointerException ... app-2
14:10:05 LB: 0 healthy backends
14:51:10 rollback to v411 complete

The deploy pipeline had no canary.
questions.promptHtml: Review the incident. What was wrong with the availability math and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the developer and adds a test for that line.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why 30 s between instances? What health check triggered? How long to detect and to decide to roll back?
  2. Immediate mitigation (in the incident): Roll back first, diagnose later; detection to rollback took 41 minutes.
  3. Hypotheses (for the gap): Failures were correlated: same code, same deploy.
  4. How I'd verify: 1 - (0.01 x 0.01) assumes independence; with a shared deploy the effective availability is bounded by the deploy failure rate, not by the product.
  5. Root cause: Shared fate in the change path plus slow detect and no automated rollback.
  6. Fix: Canary 5% with automatic rollback on SLO burn; stagger across failure domains; feature flags for risky paths; auto-rollback on health regression; also test the nightly job path.
  7. Prevention: Postmortem action items with owners; error-budget freeze; "correlated failure" section in design reviews.
  8. Trade-offs: Canaries slow deploys by minutes; worth it. I would not reduce this to "write more tests".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The bug only appears with the nightly job? -> Canary needs representative traffic; replay or synthetic of that path.
  • Rollback needs a DB migration undo? -> Make migrations backward compatible (expand/contract).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet of 40 instances was perfectly redundant against hardware and down together on every bad release until deploys became a 1%, 10%, 50% ladder.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames code.
  • Hire: names correlated failure and adds canary.
  • Strong hire: addresses detection time, auto-rollback, shared-fate review.

questions.contextHtml: On-call receives about 40 pages a week from "error rate > 1% for 5 minutes" for a service with SLO 99.9% / 30 days. Most pages auto-resolve in under 10 minutes. Last week a slow leak ran at 0.25% errors for 5 days with no page; the monthly budget was 60% gone by the time someone noticed. Traffic is 1,000 req/s.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise the threshold to 2%", which makes the slow leak even less visible.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which SLI? Are errors bursty or constant? Who gets paged vs ticketed? Do we have recording rules at several windows?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Mute the flapping alert after capturing it as a ticket; investigate the slow leak now.
  3. Hypotheses: The threshold alert is noisy for brief spikes and blind to slow burns because 0.25% never exceeds 1%.
  4. How I'd verify: Budget is 0.1%; the leak burns at 0.25 / 0.1 = 2.5x, so over 5 days it uses 2.5 x 5/30 = 42% of budget; the noisy spikes burn very little each.
  5. Root cause: The alert is not tied to budget consumption.
  6. Fix: Multi-window, multi-burn-rate: page at burn 14.4 over 1 h and 5 min (2% of budget in 1 h); page at burn 6 over 6 h and 30 min; ticket at burn 1 over 3 days and 6 h (verify numbers against the SRE workbook). The 2.5x leak triggers the 3-day ticket after a day or so.
  7. Prevention: SLO dashboard with remaining budget; review alerts quarterly.
  8. Trade-offs: More alerts to configure and explain; but each pages for a reason. I would not just raise thresholds.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Low traffic service (1 req/s)? -> A single failure moves the ratio hugely; use longer windows or a minimum volume.
  • Multiple services share one SLO? -> Alert on the user-facing SLI, not each component.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving to burn-rate alerts cut weekly pages from dozens to a handful and caught a slow memory-leak error pattern two days earlier.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks the threshold.
  • Hire: burn-rate with two windows.
  • Strong hire: computes budget use of both noisy and slow cases and covers low-traffic edge.
